idiom_name: pybreaker.CircuitBreaker(fail_max, reset_timeout) as decorator, call() or calling()
implementation_notes: pybreaker is the canonical synchronous realization: one CircuitBreaker(fail_max, reset_timeout, exclude=[...]) per integration point, applied as a decorator, through breaker.call(func, *args) or as a context manager with breaker.calling(); it opens after the configured number of consecutive failures, fails fast with CircuitBreakerError, lets the next call through after reset_timeout, and offers listeners (CircuitBreakerListener.before_call/state_change/failure/success), a success_threshold for closing, generator guarding, an optional Tornado path and a Redis-backed state storage so several worker processes share one circuit. Python has no breaker in the standard library, so a library is the realization; the differences from a hand-written counter are failure classification through exclude (types or predicates) and the listener hooks that make transitions observable.
pitfalls: pybreaker is synchronous: calling a breaker from asyncio blocks the event loop on every guarded call, so async code should use the aiobreaker variant instead.
exclude is the classifier; without it every raised exception (including validation errors) counts toward the trip threshold.

State is per process by default, so multi-worker deployments (gunicorn, Celery) each keep their own circuit and the dependency sees N times the failing calls unless a shared state storage is configured.
A success_threshold above 1 means a single healthy call does not close the breaker, and rescuers that catch broad exception types can swallow the short-circuit error together with real failures.

variants.name: aiobreaker asyncio-native CircuitBreaker
variants.idiom_name: aiobreaker.CircuitBreaker applied to async def functions with async listeners
variants.implementation_notes: aiobreaker is the asyncio fork of pybreaker: CircuitBreaker(fail_max, reset_timeout=timedelta(...)) is applied directly to async def functions, the state is kept with the running loop instead of blocking primitives, redis backing is available, and listeners may be synchronous or asynchronous so metrics collection does not block the loop. It replaces the threading-oriented structure with suspension - nothing blocks while the breaker is closed or open - but the same decisions remain: classification of excluded business exceptions, one instance per dependency at module scope, and a timeout on the guarded call, since the breaker bounds willingness and not duration.
variants.code_sketch:
from datetime import timedelta
from aiobreaker import CircuitBreaker

payments = CircuitBreaker(
    fail_max=5, reset_timeout=timedelta(seconds=30),
    exclude=[DeclinedError],                     # business errors never trip the circuit
)

@payments
async def authorize(order):
    async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=1.0) as client:     # bound the call
        return await client.post("/authorize", json=order)

# open: raises CircuitBreakerError without creating a request
pitfalls: The fail-fast error is raised inside the coroutine, so a retry wrapper catching broad exception types will treat the short circuit as transient and retry it; exclude it explicitly.
Create one breaker per dependency at module scope: constructing it per request discards the counters and never trips.
Sharing one breaker across dependencies merges failure domains, because the state is a single circuit for every call routed through it.
Redis-backed state adds an I/O dependency on the failure path: when the store itself is unreachable, the breaker's own bookkeeping becomes the outage.
